claim: Overexpression of pentacyclic triterpene synthase 1 (PEN1) in transgenic Arabidopsis thaliana plants led to significant resistance against Plutella xylostella.
source: Our analysis of transgenic Arabidopsis thaliana plants showed that overexpression of pentacyclic triterpene synthase 1, encoding the key biosynthetic enzyme for the natural plant product (3E)-4,8-dimethyl-1,3,7-nonatriene (DMNT), led to a significant resistance against a major insect pest, Plutella xylostella.
evidence: The abstract states this finding directly, and Figure 1A-C shows experimental data supporting this claim.

claim: PEN1 encodes the key biosynthetic enzyme for DMNT.
source: Our analysis of transgenic Arabidopsis thaliana plants showed that overexpression of pentacyclic triterpene synthase 1, encoding the key biosynthetic enzyme for the natural plant product (3E)-4,8-dimethyl-1,3,7-nonatriene (DMNT), led to a significant resistance against a major insect pest, Plutella xylostella.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states PEN1 encodes the key biosynthetic enzyme for DMNT, and this is supported by citation to Sohrabi et al., 2015.

claim: DMNT treatment severely damaged the peritrophic matrix (PM) in P. xylostella.
source: DMNT treatment severely damaged the peritrophic matrix (PM), a physical barrier isolating food and pathogens from the midgut wall cells.
evidence: The abstract states this directly, and Figures 3A-H show microscopy data demonstrating PM damage.

claim: The peritrophic matrix is a physical barrier isolating food and pathogens from the midgut wall cells.
source: DMNT treatment severely damaged the peritrophic matrix (PM), a physical barrier isolating food and pathogens from the midgut wall cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is consistent with established knowledge about PM function.

claim: DMNT repressed the expression of PxMucin in midgut cells.
source: DMNT repressed the expression of PxMucin in midgut cells, and knocking down PxMucin resulted in PM rupture and P. xylostella death.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, and Figure 4B-C shows qRT-PCR data demonstrating downregulation of PxMucin.

claim: Knocking down PxMucin resulted in PM rupture and P. xylostella death.
source: DMNT repressed the expression of PxMucin in midgut cells, and knocking down PxMucin resulted in PM rupture and P. xylostella death.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, and Figure 4F-K shows experimental data from RNAi experiments.

claim: DMNT significantly disrupted midgut microbiota populations in P. xylostella.
source: A 16S RNA survey revealed that DMNT significantly disrupted midgut microbiota populations and that midgut microbes were essential for DMNT-induced killing.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, and Figure 6A-B shows 16S rDNA sequencing data demonstrating changes in microbiota composition.

claim: Midgut microbes are essential for DMNT-induced killing of P. xylostella.
source: A 16S RNA survey revealed that DMNT significantly disrupted midgut microbiota populations and that midgut microbes were essential for DMNT-induced killing.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, and Figure 5C-D shows that antibiotic treatment eliminates DMNT toxicity.

claim: The midgut microbiota assists DMNT in killing P. xylostella.
source: Therefore, we propose that the midgut microbiota assists DMNT in killing P. xylostella.
evidence: This is proposed based on the experimental findings showing that antibiotics eliminate DMNT toxicity while PM damage persists.

claim: Plutella xylostella has been ranked as one of the most difficult pests to control due to its short life cycle, high migration rate, strong tolerance to environmental stresses, and rising resistance to available insecticides.
source: The diamondback moth Plutella xylostella (Lepidoptera: Plutellidae) has been ranked as one of the most difficult pests to control due to its short life cycle, high migration rate, strong tolerance to environmental stresses, and rising resistance to available insecticides (Shakeel et al., 2017; Vaschetto and Beccacece, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Shakeel et al., 2017 and Vaschetto and Beccacece, 2019.

claim: An estimated 4-5 billion dollars are devoted each year to control of P. xylostella worldwide.
source: An estimated 4–5 billion dollars are devoted each year to control of this pest worldwide (Zalucki et al., 2012).
evidence: This economic estimate is supported by citation to Zalucki et al., 2012.

claim: PEN1 has been reported to be a key enzyme in the biosynthesis of the volatile homoterpene DMNT.
source: PEN1 has been reported to be a key enzyme in the biosynthesis of the volatile homoterpene DMNT (Sohrabi et al., 2015), which was confirmed by our gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) analysis on 35Spro:PEN1 transgenic plants.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sohrabi et al., 2015 and confirmed by GC-MS data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: DMNT was enriched and could be highly induced by P. xylostella infestation in 35Spro:PEN1 transgenic plants.
source: DMNT was enriched and could be highly induced by P. xylostella infestation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D), suggesting that DMNT might play a role in plant resistance against this chewing insect.
evidence: This is demonstrated by GC-MS data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-D.

claim: P. xylostella larvae fed on 35Spro:PEN1 transgenic plants showed significantly lower survival rate than those on the non-transgenic control.
source: the P. xylostella larvae fed on 35Spro:PEN1 transgenic plants showed significantly lower survival rate than those on the non-transgenic control (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C with statistical significance indicated.

claim: Much less of the DMNT-treated leaves was eaten compared to the control leaves.
source: To validate this hypothesis, we synthesized DMNT and sprayed the chemical on Brassica napus leaves before feeding of P. xylostella larvae; this bioassay demonstrated that much less of the DMNT-treated leaves was eaten compared to the control leaves (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the bioassay shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Significantly more P. xylostella larvae moved away from the DMNT side after 10-120 min in preference tests.
source: As shown in Figure 1E, significantly more larvae moved away from the DMNT side after 10–120 min, indicating that P. xylostella larvae perceived and avoided the DMNT (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1E with statistical significance indicated.

claim: P. xylostella larvae perceived and avoided DMNT.
source: As shown in Figure 1E, significantly more larvae moved away from the DMNT side after 10–120 min, indicating that P. xylostella larvae perceived and avoided the DMNT (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is inferred from the preference test data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Exposure to DMNT for 48 hr resulted in the death of ~20% of larvae, which increased to 50% after 120 hr.
source: Indeed, exposure to DMNT for 48 hr resulted in the death of ~20% of larvae, which increased to 50% after 120 hr; meanwhile, the larva growth and pupation rates were also severely affected (Figure 1F–I).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1F with survival data over time.

claim: DMNT exposure severely affected larva growth and pupation rates.
source: Indeed, exposure to DMNT for 48 hr resulted in the death of ~20% of larvae, which increased to 50% after 120 hr; meanwhile, the larva growth and pupation rates were also severely affected (Figure 1F–I).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 1G-I with data on growth and pupation.

claim: DMNT showed no significant dose-dependent effects on the survival or pupation of P. xylostella larvae at concentrations of 0.7, 7, or 70 μM.
source: Although the overall survival and pupation rates of P. xylostella larvae significantly decreased at all concentrations, we observed no significant effect of dosage (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A, B), in agreement with results obtained with the root-rot pathogen Pythium irregulare (Sohrabi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-B and is consistent with findings from Sohrabi et al., 2015.

claim: DMNT significantly affected all stages of P. xylostella larvae tested (first- to fourth-instar), although first- and second-instar larvae had a more pronounced response.
source: Accordingly, we fed first- to fourth-instar larvae with forage containing DMNT, which revealed that DMNT significantly affected all stages of P. xylostella larvae tested in these assays, although first- and second-instar larvae had a more pronounced response relative to other stages (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4 with data for different larval stages.

claim: P. xylostella larvae displayed significantly lower forage intake and less defecation when treated with DMNT.
source: P. xylostella larvae appeared to display significantly lower forage intake and less defecation when treated with DMNT (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A–D), raising the possibility that P. xylostella larvae might be dying from starvation.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A-D with measurements of forage intake and defecation.

claim: DMNT-treated P. xylostella larvae died at least 12 hr earlier than those experiencing starvation.
source: As shown in Figure 2A, DMNT-treated P. xylostella larvae died at least 12 hr earlier than those experiencing starvation.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A comparing mortality rates over time.

claim: Starved larvae had much smaller bodies at the time of death relative to DMNT-treated larvae.
source: In addition, starved larvae had much smaller bodies at the time of death relative to DMNT-treated larvae (Figure 1—figure supplement 5E), indicating that P. xylostella larvae were likely quickly poisoned to death by DMNT rather than being killed by DMNT-induced starvation.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5E and used to infer the mechanism of death.

claim: P. xylostella larvae were likely quickly poisoned to death by DMNT rather than being killed by DMNT-induced starvation.
source: In addition, starved larvae had much smaller bodies at the time of death relative to DMNT-treated larvae (Figure 1—figure supplement 5E), indicating that P. xylostella larvae were likely quickly poisoned to death by DMNT rather than being killed by DMNT-induced starvation.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of body sizes and mortality timing between DMNT-treated and starved larvae.

claim: DMNT-treated larvae showed significantly lower lipase activity compared to controls.
source: When compared to the controls, DMNT-treated larvae showed significantly lower lipase activity, suggesting that their gut function was indeed disrupted (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B with lipase activity measurements.

claim: The gut function of DMNT-treated larvae was disrupted.
source: When compared to the controls, DMNT-treated larvae showed significantly lower lipase activity, suggesting that their gut function was indeed disrupted (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced lipase activity shown in Figure 2B.

claim: DMNT treatment resulted in three times as many Smurf larvae as no Smurf larvae.
source: A quantitative assessment of blue (Smurf) and normal (no Smurf) larvae showed that DMNT treatment resulted in three times as many Smurf larvae as no Smurf larvae (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E with quantification of Smurf phenotype.

claim: DMNT caused lesions at the larval midgut and resulted in higher permeability.
source: These results suggested that DMNT caused lesions at the larval midgut and resulted in higher permeability.
evidence: This is inferred from the Smurf test results showing dye retention in DMNT-treated larvae.

claim: After DMNT treatment for 48 hr, the PM became thin and loose, whereas the PM of control samples remained intact and plump.
source: After DMNT treatment for 48 hr, the PM became thin and loose, whereas the PM of control samples remained intact and plump (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A-B with stereomicroscope images of dissected PM.

claim: The PM of larvae treated with DMNT for 24 hr was thin and discontinuous in some regions.
source: Hematoxylin-eosin (HE) staining revealed that the PM of control larvae was thick and intact (Figure 3C, E), whereas the PM of larvae treated with DMNT for 24 hr was thin and discontinuous in some regions (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D with HE staining of transverse sections.

claim: After 48 hr of exposure to DMNT, the PM was completely corrupted and the intestinal content got close to the intestine wall, with several enterocyte cells spilling from the epithelial wall.
source: This effect became more pronounced after 48 hr of exposure to DMNT as the PM was completely corrupted and the intestinal content got close to the intestine wall, with several enterocyte cells spilling from the epithelial wall (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3F with HE staining of transverse sections.

claim: After 12 hr DMNT treatment, there were 189 genes differentially expressed with a minimum cutoff of twofold change; among these 189 genes, 62 were upregulated and 127 were downregulated.
source: Compared with the control, after 12 hr DMNT treatment, there were 189 genes differentially expressed with a minimum cutoff of twofold change; among these 189 genes, 62 were upregulated and 127 were downregulated (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is from RNA-seq analysis with results provided in Supplementary file 1.

claim: PxMucin encodes a mucin-like protein that accumulates in the PM.
source: A gene PxMucin, encoding a mucin-like protein, caught our attention as its protein was reported to accumulate in the PM (Sarauer et al., 2003; Israni and Rajam, 2017; Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sarauer et al., 2003 and Israni and Rajam, 2017.

claim: After DMNT treatment for 48 hr, PxMucin transcript levels were significantly downregulated compared to control larvae.
source: After DMNT treatment for 48 hr, PxMucin transcript levels were significantly downregulated compared to control larvae (Figure 4B, C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B-C with qRT-PCR data.

claim: dsRNA against PxMucin significantly downregulated endogenous PxMucin in the dsRNA-fed larvae.
source: This dsRNA significantly downregulated endogenous PxMucin in the dsRNA-fed larvae (Figure 4D, E) and resulted in a significant reduction in growth, survival, and pupation rates, as well as lighter larval bodies (Figure 4F–I).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D-E with qRT-PCR data confirming RNAi knockdown.

claim: dsRNA against PxMucin resulted in a significant reduction in growth, survival, and pupation rates, as well as lighter larval bodies.
source: This dsRNA significantly downregulated endogenous PxMucin in the dsRNA-fed larvae (Figure 4D, E) and resulted in a significant reduction in growth, survival, and pupation rates, as well as lighter larval bodies (Figure 4F–I).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4F-I with measurements of various developmental parameters.

claim: Transverse sections of dsRNA-fed larvae indicated that the PM structure became thin and disappeared in some regions.
source: Furthermore, transverse sections of dsRNA-fed larvae indicated that the PM structure became thin and disappeared in some regions (Figure 4J, K), observations that were similar to the DMNT-treated larva (Figure 3), suggesting that DMNT may disrupt the PM partially through the repression of PxMucin expression.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4J-K with HE staining of transverse sections.

claim: DMNT may disrupt the PM partially through the repression of PxMucin expression.
source: Furthermore, transverse sections of dsRNA-fed larvae indicated that the PM structure became thin and disappeared in some regions (Figure 4J, K), observations that were similar to the DMNT-treated larva (Figure 3), suggesting that DMNT may disrupt the PM partially through the repression of PxMucin expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity between PxMucin RNAi and DMNT treatment phenotypes.

claim: Antibiotic treatment had no significant influence on the survival or pupation rates of P. xylostella larvae.
source: In contrast to the results obtained in mosquito, antibiotic treatment had no significant influence on the survival or pupation rates of P. xylostella larvae (Figure 5A, B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A-B with survival and pupation data.

claim: The PM was intact even after the removal of the midgut microbiota by the antibiotic cocktail.
source: Consistent with this observation, transverse section and HE staining indicated that the PM was intact even after the removal of the midgut microbiota by the antibiotic cocktail, suggesting that the formation and/or maintenance of the P. xylostella PM are not dependent on the midgut microbiota (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 with HE staining of transverse sections.

claim: The formation and/or maintenance of the P. xylostella PM are not dependent on the midgut microbiota.
source: Consistent with this observation, transverse section and HE staining indicated that the PM was intact even after the removal of the midgut microbiota by the antibiotic cocktail, suggesting that the formation and/or maintenance of the P. xylostella PM are not dependent on the midgut microbiota (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that antibiotics do not affect PM integrity.

claim: The effects of DMNT on P. xylostella were completely abolished upon the addition of antibiotics.
source: Our results indicated that the effects of DMNT on P. xylostella were completely abolished upon the addition of antibiotics (Figure 5C, D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C-D with survival and pupation data for combined treatments.

claim: The midgut section showed a similarly damaged PM structure upon treatment with either DMNT alone, or with the combination of DMNT and antibiotics.
source: Quite on the contrary, the midgut section showed a similarly damaged PM structure upon treatment with either DMNT alone, or with the combination of DMNT and antibiotics, suggesting that an active population of gut microbiota contributes to the DMNT-induced PM damage that kills larvae, but that gut microbiota do not directly affect the PM (Figure 5E–H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E-H with HE staining of transverse sections.

claim: An active population of gut microbiota contributes to the DMNT-induced PM damage that kills larvae, but gut microbiota do not directly affect the PM.
source: Quite on the contrary, the midgut section showed a similarly damaged PM structure upon treatment with either DMNT alone, or with the combination of DMNT and antibiotics, suggesting that an active population of gut microbiota contributes to the DMNT-induced PM damage that kills larvae, but that gut microbiota do not directly affect the PM (Figure 5E–H).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that antibiotics prevent death but not PM damage.

claim: The midgut microbiota could pass the PM barrier and invade midgut cells more easily when the PM was damaged by DMNT compared to controls.
source: In addition, we determined that the midgut microbiota could pass the PM barrier and invade midgut cells more easily when the PM was damaged by DMNT compared to controls (Figure 5I, J).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5I-J with Gram staining showing bacterial invasion.

claim: DMNT treatment significantly disturbed the microbiota composition in the midgut of P. xylostella larvae.
source: A principal component analysis of midgut microbes based on 16S ribosomal DNA sequencing indicated that the DMNT treatment significantly disturbed the microbiota composition in the midgut of P. xylostella larvae (Figure 6A, B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1), with the abundance of 18 phyla, such as proteobacteria and firmicutes, showing strong changes after DMNT treatment (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A-B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1 with 16S rDNA sequencing data.

claim: The firmicutes bacterium Enterococcus was enriched around 85-fold in DMNT-treated larvae relative to the control.
source: As an example, the firmicutes bacterium Enterococcus was enriched around 85-fold in DMNT-treated larvae relative to the control (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2 with 16S rDNA sequencing data.

claim: Feeding with gut microbes significantly decreased the survival or pupation rates of antibiotics-treated larvae compared with the antibiotics-treated controls.
source: Without DMNT, gut microbe feeding significantly decreased the survival or pupation rates of the larvae compared with the antibiotics-treated controls, and strikingly the addition of gut microbes alongside DMNT strongly enhanced the effects of DMNT treatment, all larvae died at 120 hr, and no larvae pupated in the end (Figure 6C, D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C-D with survival and pupation data.

claim: The addition of gut microbes alongside DMNT strongly enhanced the effects of DMNT treatment, with all larvae dying at 120 hr and no larvae pupating.
source: Without DMNT, gut microbe feeding significantly decreased the survival or pupation rates of the larvae compared with the antibiotics-treated controls, and strikingly the addition of gut microbes alongside DMNT strongly enhanced the effects of DMNT treatment, all larvae died at 120 hr, and no larvae pupated in the end (Figure 6C, D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C-D with survival and pupation data.

claim: The lysozyme expression of larvae gut was significantly downregulated from 48 to 72 hr after DMNT treatment.
source: RT-PCR results showed that the lysozyme expression of larvae gut was significantly downregulated from 48 to 72 hr after DMNT treatment, suggesting that DMNT-treated larvae had a weakened ability to resist pathogen invasions (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4 with qRT-PCR data.

claim: DMNT-treated larvae had a weakened ability to resist pathogen invasions.
source: RT-PCR results showed that the lysozyme expression of larvae gut was significantly downregulated from 48 to 72 hr after DMNT treatment, suggesting that DMNT-treated larvae had a weakened ability to resist pathogen invasions (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is inferred from the downregulation of lysozyme expression.

claim: The natural plant compound DMNT can serve as an effective bioinsecticide against P. xylostella.
source: In this study, we present strong evidence that the natural plant compound DMNT can serve as an effective bioinsecticide against P. xylostella.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from all the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: DMNT exposure damages the PM structure in a microbiota-assisted manner, partially by repressing the expression of PxMucin.
source: DMNT exposure damages the PM structure in a microbiota-assisted manner, partially by repressing the expression of PxMucin.
evidence: This is the mechanistic conclusion drawn from the combined experimental results.

claim: The PM consists of a mixture of chitin and glycoproteins secreted by intestinal cells that serves as a first and essential barrier to isolate food and intestinal microbes from the intestinal cells of invertebrates.
source: The PM consists of a mixture of chitin and glycoproteins secreted by intestinal cells that serves as a first and essential barrier to isolate food and intestinal microbes from the intestinal cells of invertebrates such as Bombyx mori, H. armigera, Anopheles gambiae, and Drosophila melanogaster (Hegedus et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Hegedus et al., 2019 and Liu et al., 2019.

claim: The PM prevents tissue infections in the midgut of insects.
source: The PM therefore prevents tissue infections in the midgut of insects (Dinglasan et al., 2009; Erlandson et al., 2019; Hegedus et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Dinglasan et al., 2009, Erlandson et al., 2019, and Hegedus et al., 2019.

claim: In fruit fly (D. melanogaster), the protein drosocrystallin is a central component of the PM whose loss of function results in a reduction of PM width and an increase in its permeability, leading to higher sensitivity to bacterial infection from intestinal contents.
source: In fruit fly (D. melanogaster), the protein drosocrystallin is a central component of the PM whose loss of function results in a reduction of PM width and an increase in its permeability, leading to higher sensitivity to bacterial infection from intestinal contents (Kuraishi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kuraishi et al., 2011.

claim: The mucin-like protein Mucin was reported to locate to the PM and plays important roles as a saliva component involved in the virulence, host adaptation, and immunity response of the brown planthopper (Nilaparvata lugens).
source: The mucin-like protein Mucin was reported to locate to the PM and plays important roles as a saliva component involved in the virulence, host adaptation, and immunity response of the brown planthopper (Nilaparvata lugens) (Huang et al., 2017; Shangguan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Huang et al., 2017 and Shangguan et al., 2018.

claim: In maize, some cultivars develop a sharp epidermis on their leaf surface that can cause the PM of the fall armyworm (Spodoptera frugiperda) to rupture; this was proposed to be one of the mechanisms leading to pest death.
source: In maize, some cultivars develop a sharp epidermis on their leaf surface that can cause the PM of the fall armyworm (Spodoptera frugiperda) to rupture; this was proposed to be one of the mechanisms leading to pest death (Mason et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mason et al., 2019.

claim: In mosquito Anopheles coluzzii, the formation or maintenance of the PM depends on the midgut microbiota, and the PM ruptured when antibiotics were added to the blood meal and killed the microbiota.
source: In mosquito Anopheles coluzzii, the formation or maintenance of the PM depends on the midgut microbiota, and the PM ruptured when antibiotics were added to the blood meal and killed the microbiota (Rodgers et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rodgers et al., 2017.

claim: Mosquitoes became more susceptible to infections from the Plasmodium parasite or dengue viruses when their midgut microbiota was cleared.
source: In agreement, several studies showed that mosquitoes became more susceptible to infections from the Plasmodium parasite or dengue viruses when their midgut microbiota was cleared, even though the exact causal mechanism remains elusive (Dong et al., 2009; Wei et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dong et al., 2009 and Wei et al., 2017.

claim: DMNT can be used as an insect repellent, driving pests away from plants following application.
source: This characteristic is critical and suggests that DMNT can be used as an insect repellent, driving pests away from plants following application.
evidence: This is inferred from the preference test data showing larvae avoid DMNT.

claim: Upon damage incurred by the PM in response to DMNT exposure, pathogens residing in the midgut pass through the PM lesions and invade midgut epithelial cells, leading to infection and tissue inflammation.
source: We propose the following model: upon damage incurred by the PM in response to DMNT exposure (Figure 3), pathogens residing in the midgut pass through the PM lesions and invade midgut epithelial cells, leading to infection and tissue inflammation.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental observations.

claim: DMNT treatment severely affected the midgut environment, causing a reduction in the dominant bacterial populations seen in controls, whereas Enterococcus populations substantially increased.
source: Furthermore, the analysis of microbiota populations showed that DMNT treatment severely affected the midgut environment, causing a reduction in the dominant bacterial populations seen in controls, whereas Enterococcus populations substantially increased (Figure 6A, B, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A-B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2 with 16S rDNA sequencing data.

claim: Plants may regulate microbial communities by releasing volatile compounds.
source: Several terpenoid compounds have recently been reported to selectively modulate the Arabidopsis root microbiota (Huang et al., 2019). It suggests that plants may regulate microbial communities by releasing volatile compounds.
evidence: This is inferred from the citation to Huang et al., 2019 and the current study's findings.

claim: DMNT may damage the PM and affect pest growth by regulating several signaling pathways related to PM formation rather than through a simple physical interaction with the PM.
source: RNAi-based knockdown of this gene led to a defect in the PM structure, lower pupation rate, and larval death (Figure 4), suggesting that DMNT may damage the PM and affect pest growth by regulating several signaling pathways related to PM formation rather than through a simple physical interaction with the PM.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNAi results showing that gene expression changes lead to PM damage.

claim: The ability of DMNT to affect the PM structure and kill insect pests requires the assistance of the microbiota from the insect midgut and may represent a general phenomenon in other organisms.
source: In conclusion, we described the interplay between the natural metabolite DMNT, midgut microbiota, and insect host death. The ability of DMNT to affect the PM structure and kill insect pests requires the assistance of the microbiota from the insect midgut and may represent a general phenomenon in other organisms that explains how the intestinal microbiota is prevented from infecting their hosts.
evidence: This is the main conclusion and speculation about broader implications.

claim: The volatile homoterpene compound (3E)-4,8-dimethyl-1,3,7-nonatriene (DMNT) mediates plant–plant communication in sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas) and triggers systemic and jasmonic acid (JA)-independent anti-herbivore defenses in neighboring plants.
source: For example, the volatile homoterpene compound (3E)-4,8-dimethyl-1,3,7-nonatriene (DMNT) mediates plant–plant communication in sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas) and triggers systemic and jasmonic acid (JA)-independent anti-herbivore defenses in neighboring plants. These plants are induced to synthesize the protease inhibitor and storage protein sporamin, which is toxic to chewing pests (Meents et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Meents et al., 2019.

claim: Exposure of Spodoptera exigua larva to herbivore-induced plant volatiles (HIPVs) such as indole increased its susceptibility to nucleopolyhedrovirus and Bacillus thuringiensis.
source: Gasmi and colleagues reported that exposure of Spodoptera exigua larva to herbivore-induced plant volatiles (HIPVs) such as indole increased its susceptibility to nucleopolyhedrovirus and Bacillus thuringiensis, and additionally they found that the microbiota population in larval midgut was significantly affected, but the mechanism remains unclear (Gasmi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gasmi et al., 2019.

claim: Various HIPVs including indole have been reported to show direct toxicity to beet armyworm.
source: Another major line of plant defense relies on the ability to kill pests directly via the secretion of natural products that are harmful to insects. For instance, various HIPVs including indole have been reported to show direct toxicity to beet armyworm (Maurya et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Maurya et al., 2020.

claim: Some maize (Zea mays L.) ecotypes produce a 33 kDa cysteine protease in response to caterpillar feeding that damages the insect intestine, leading to death.
source: Some maize (Zea mays L.) ecotypes produce a 33 kDa cysteine protease in response to caterpillar feeding that damages the insect intestine, leading to death (Pechan et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pechan et al., 2002.

claim: Several members of the Rubiaceae and Violaceae families produce cyclotides or macrocyclic peptides of 28–37 amino acids that disrupt epithelial cells in the midgut of cotton bollworm (Helicoverpa armigera).
source: Several members of the Rubiaceae and Violaceae families produce cyclotides or macrocyclic peptides of 28–37 amino acids that disrupt epithelial cells in the midgut of cotton bollworm (Helicoverpa armigera) (Barbeta et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Barbeta et al., 2008.

claim: The secondary metabolite benzoxazinoids are produced in crops, provide resistance against a broad spectrum of pests, and are used as a resistance marker in crops.
source: Another effective defense compound is the secondary metabolite benzoxazinoids, which are produced in crops, provide resistance against a broad spectrum of pests, and are used as a resistance marker in crops (Robert et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Robert et al., 2017.

claim: The insect midgut and the peritrophic matrix (PM) structure are the main targets of insecticides.
source: Mounting evidence shows that the insect midgut and the peritrophic matrix (PM) structure are the main targets of insecticides (Kuraishi et al., 2011; Song et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kuraishi et al., 2011 and Song et al., 2018.

claim: DMNT in A. thaliana plants can be continuously induced by P. xylostella infestation, accumulating to ~70 ng/g after 3–21 hr.
source: Considering the fact that DMNT in A. thaliana plants can be continuously induced by P. xylostella infestation, accumulating to ~70 ng/g after 3–21 hr (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D), and in contrast DMNT injected in forage for bioassays will become less due to volatilizing along with the process of experiments, we selected the dosage of 7 μM DMNT for further studies.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-D with GC-MS measurements.

claim: The dsRNA against PxMucin likely has low off-target effects, and the developmental defects of the dsRNA-treated P. xylostella larvae were mainly caused by the downregulation of PxMucin.
source: These results suggest that the dsRNA against PxMucin likely has low off-target, and the developmental defects of the dsRNA-treated P. xylostella larvae were mainly caused by the downregulation of PxMucin.
evidence: This is inferred from the qRT-PCR analysis showing no significant changes in homologous genes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).

claim: There was no significant difference in the expression levels of peritrophin 1 like, chondroitin proteoglycan 2 like, and mucin 2 like between the dsRNA-treated and non-treated control.
